OverallSummary:
This case involves Edward Scott Short, a former General Securities Representative associated with Laidlaw & Company (UK) Ltd., who engaged in excessive trading in an elderly customer's account. The excessive trading occurred between July 2018 and December 2020, with Short making 204 transaction recommendations that generated $116,859 in commissions while causing approximately $185,000 in trading losses. FINRA found that Short violated Regulation BI's Care Obligation after it went into effect on June 30, 2020, and FINRA Rule 2111 before that date.

The excessive trading was identified through quantitative analysis showing extremely high metrics: an annualized cost-to-equity ratio of 76.53% (meaning the account needed to grow by more than 76% annually just to break even) and an annualized turnover rate of 47.49. FINRA notes that a turnover rate of 6 or a cost-to-equity ratio above 20% generally indicates excessive trading. These metrics far exceeded these thresholds.

Short exercised de facto control over the 77-year-old customer's account, as the customer routinely followed Short's recommendations. Though the customer had a high net worth and a speculative investment objective, the level of trading was deemed excessive, unsuitable, and not in the customer's best interest. As a result, Short was suspended for seven months, fined $5,000, and ordered to pay $116,859 in restitution plus interest to the affected customer. The case also resulted in a statutory disqualification due to the willful violation of Regulation BI.
